subproblems.title: Borel measurability of the exceptional set of the generalized cone trichotomy along a continuous family (Steps 1 and 4.2)
subproblems.statement: Let n, ℓ ∈ ℕ, E := ℝ^{n+ℓ} = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (n+ℓ)), Hⁿ := μHE[n], and let X be a finite-dimensional real normed space with its Borel σ-algebra. Let A ⊆ E be compact with Hⁿ(A) < ∞, δ > 0, α : X → E continuous, and F₁, F₂ : X → E → E such that (ξ, y) ↦ F₁ ξ y and (ξ, y) ↦ F₂ ξ y are continuous on X × E. For ξ ∈ X and r, s ∈ ℝ let C(ξ, r, s) := {x : |F₁ ξ (x − αξ)| < s|F₂ ξ (x − αξ)|} ∩ B(αξ, r) and m(ξ, r, s) := Hⁿ(A ∩ C(ξ, r, s)). Say GT(ξ) holds if one of the following holds. (Φ0) For every c > 0 there is ε > 0 with m(ξ, r, s) ≤ c(rs)ⁿ for all 0 < s < ε and 0 < r < δ. (Φ∞) For every K ∈ ℝ and ε > 0 there are 0 < s < ε and 0 < r < δ with K(rs)ⁿ ≤ m(ξ, r, s). (Ax) Some b ∈ A has b ≠ αξ, |b − αξ| < δ and F₁ ξ (b − αξ) = 0. Numerical bounds are compared in [0, ∞] via ENNReal.ofReal. Then {ξ ∈ X : αξ ∈ A and not GT(ξ)} is a measurable (Borel) subset of X.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) {X : Type} [NormedAddCommGroup X] [NormedSpace ℝ X] [FiniteDimensional ℝ X] [MeasurableSpace X] [BorelSpace X] (A : Set (Rn (n + ℓ))), IsCompact A → μHE[n] A < ∞ → ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → ∀ (α : X → Rn (n + ℓ)) (F₁ F₂ : X → Rn (n + ℓ) → Rn (n + ℓ)), Continuous α → Continuous (fun q : X × Rn (n + ℓ) ↦ F₁ q.1 q.2) → Continuous (fun q : X × Rn (n + ℓ) ↦ F₂ q.1 q.2) → MeasurableSet {ξ : X | α ξ ∈ A ∧ ¬ ((∀ c : ℝ, 0 < c → ∃ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε ∧ ∀ s : ℝ, 0 < s → s < ε → ∀ r : ℝ, 0 < r → r < δ → μHE[n] (A ∩ ({x | ‖F₁ ξ (x - α ξ)‖ < s * ‖F₂ ξ (x - α ξ)‖} ∩ Metric.ball (α ξ) r)) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (c * (r * s) ^ n)) ∨ (∀ K : ℝ, ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ s : ℝ, 0 < s ∧ s < ε ∧ ∃ r : ℝ, 0 < r ∧ r < δ ∧ ENNReal.ofReal (K * (r * s) ^ n) ≤ μHE[n] (A ∩ ({x | ‖F₁ ξ (x - α ξ)‖ < s * ‖F₂ ξ (x - α ξ)‖} ∩ Metric.ball (α ξ) r))) ∨ ∃ b ∈ A, b ≠ (α ξ) ∧ dist b (α ξ) < δ ∧ F₁ ξ (b - α ξ) = 0)}
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Step 1 (1.1–1.4) of the supplied proof of the cone trichotomy (parent Step 8a; Mattila, Geometry of Sets and Measures in Euclidean Spaces, Ch. 18; Dall'Alba, The Besicovitch–Federer Projection Theorem, §4–5) together with its Step 4.2, which repeats the same argument for slab cones. Here the argument is written once for an arbitrary continuous family, which covers both uses. Notation: E := ℝ^{n+ℓ} = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (n+ℓ)), |·| the Euclidean norm, B(x, ρ) the open ball, Hⁿ := μHE[n], ofReal := ENNReal.ofReal; all inequalities between measures and numbers are in [0, ∞].

1. Setting. X is a finite-dimensional real normed space with its Borel σ-algebra, so X, E and X × E are proper, second-countable metric spaces. In particular the product σ-algebra of X × E is its Borel σ-algebra. A is compact, hence closed and Borel. ν(S) := Hⁿ(S ∩ A), i.e. ν := Hⁿ restricted to the Borel set A, is a Borel measure on E with ν(E) = Hⁿ(A) < ∞, so ν is finite. For ξ ∈ X and r, s ∈ ℝ put C(ξ, r, s) := {x : |F₁ ξ (x − αξ)| < s|F₂ ξ (x − αξ)|} ∩ B(αξ, r) and m(ξ, r, s) := Hⁿ(A ∩ C(ξ, r, s)). C(ξ, r, s) is open in E, because x ↦ F_i ξ (x − αξ) is continuous (i = 1, 2), so C(ξ, r, s) is Borel and m(ξ, r, s) = ν(C(ξ, r, s)). Write Φ0(ξ), Φ∞(ξ), Ax(ξ) for the three disjuncts in the statement:
 Φ0(ξ): ∀c > 0 ∃ε > 0 ∀s ∈ (0, ε) ∀r ∈ (0, δ): m(ξ, r, s) ≤ ofReal(c(rs)ⁿ);
 Φ∞(ξ): ∀K ∈ ℝ ∀ε > 0 ∃s ∈ (0, ε) ∃r ∈ (0, δ): ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) ≤ m(ξ, r, s);
 Ax(ξ): ∃b ∈ A with b ≠ αξ, dist(b, αξ) = |b − αξ| < δ and F₁ ξ (b − αξ) = 0.
 The set to be shown measurable is Z := {ξ : αξ ∈ A} ∖ ({Φ0} ∪ {Φ∞} ∪ {Ax}), where {P} := {ξ ∈ X : P(ξ)}.

2. For fixed r, s the map ξ ↦ m(ξ, r, s) is lower semicontinuous, hence Borel. Let U := {(ξ, x) ∈ X × E : |F₁ ξ (x − αξ)| < s|F₂ ξ (x − αξ)| and |x − αξ| < r}. U is open in X × E, since (ξ, x) ↦ F_i ξ (x − αξ) is the composition of the jointly continuous (ξ, y) ↦ F_i ξ y with the continuous (ξ, x) ↦ (ξ, x − αξ), and (ξ, x) ↦ |x − αξ| is continuous. Its section U_ξ := {x : (ξ, x) ∈ U} is C(ξ, r, s). Let ξ_k → ξ in X. If x ∈ U_ξ, then (ξ_k, x) ∈ U for all large k because U is open. Hence 1_{U_ξ}(x) ≤ liminf_k 1_{U_{ξ_k}}(x) for every x ∈ E. By Fatou's lemma, ν(U_ξ) = ∫1_{U_ξ} dν ≤ ∫liminf_k 1_{U_{ξ_k}} dν ≤ liminf_k ν(U_{ξ_k}). Since X is metrizable, this sequential lower semicontinuity is lower semicontinuity. So for every t ∈ [0, ∞] the set {ξ : m(ξ, r, s) > t} is open and {ξ : m(ξ, r, s) ≤ t} is closed. (Equivalently, the measurability alone follows from the measurability part of Tonelli's theorem, Mathlib measurable_measure_prodMk_left, because U is a Borel subset of X × E and ν is finite.) In particular, for all real r, s, c, K the sets {ξ : m(ξ, r, s) ≤ ofReal(c(rs)ⁿ)} and {ξ : ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) < m(ξ, r, s)} are Borel.

3. Monotonicity and left continuity in (r, s). Fix ξ. If 0 < r′ ≤ r and 0 < s′ ≤ s, then C(ξ, r′, s′) ⊆ C(ξ, r, s), because s′|F₂ ξ y| ≤ s|F₂ ξ y|. Hence m(ξ, ·, ·) is nondecreasing in each variable. Let r, s > 0. By density of ℚ choose rationals r_k, s_k (k ∈ ℕ) with 0 < r_k < r, 0 < s_k < s, both sequences nondecreasing, and r_k → r, s_k → s. For example, with r_{−1} := 0 and s_{−1} := 0, choose recursively rationals r_k ∈ (max(r_{k−1}, r − r/(k+2)), r) and s_k ∈ (max(s_{k−1}, s − s/(k+2)), s). Then C(ξ, r_k, s_k) is nondecreasing in k and ⋃_k C(ξ, r_k, s_k) = C(ξ, r, s). For “⊆” use monotonicity. For “⊇” let x ∈ C(ξ, r, s) and y := x − αξ; then 0 ≤ |F₁ ξ y| < s|F₂ ξ y|, so |F₂ ξ y| > 0. Since s_k → s, we get |F₁ ξ y| < s_k|F₂ ξ y| for all large k, and |y| < r_k for all large k; so x ∈ C(ξ, r_k, s_k) for large k. By continuity from below of ν, m(ξ, r, s) = sup_k m(ξ, r_k, s_k).

4. Countable form of Φ0. Let ℚ₊ := ℚ ∩ (0, ∞). Claim: Φ0(ξ) holds iff for every c ∈ ℚ₊ there is ε ∈ ℚ₊ such that m(ξ, r, s) ≤ ofReal(c(rs)ⁿ) for all rational s ∈ (0, ε) and rational r ∈ (0, δ). (⇒) For rational c > 0, Φ0 gives a real ε > 0; take a rational ε′ ∈ (0, ε]. Every rational s ∈ (0, ε′) and r ∈ (0, δ) is an admissible real pair. (⇐) Let c > 0 be real. Take a rational c′ ∈ (0, c] and its rational ε. Let s ∈ (0, ε) and r ∈ (0, δ) be real, and take the rational sequences r_k ↑ r, s_k ↑ s of step 3; then r_k ∈ (0, δ) and s_k ∈ (0, ε). Hence m(ξ, r_k, s_k) ≤ ofReal(c′(r_k s_k)ⁿ) ≤ ofReal(c(rs)ⁿ), because 0 < r_k s_k ≤ rs and 0 < c′ ≤ c. Taking the supremum over k gives m(ξ, r, s) ≤ ofReal(c(rs)ⁿ) by step 3. Consequently {Φ0} = ⋂_{c∈ℚ₊} ⋃_{ε∈ℚ₊} ⋂_{s∈ℚ∩(0,ε)} ⋂_{r∈ℚ∩(0,δ)} {ξ : m(ξ, r, s) ≤ ofReal(c(rs)ⁿ)}, which is Borel by step 2 (countable intersections and unions).

5. Countable form of Φ∞. Claim: Φ∞(ξ) holds iff for every K ∈ ℕ and ε ∈ ℚ₊ there are rational s ∈ (0, ε) and rational r ∈ (0, δ) with ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) < m(ξ, r, s). (⇐) Let K ∈ ℝ and ε > 0. Take a natural K′ ≥ K and a rational ε′ ∈ (0, ε]. The condition for K′ and ε′ gives s ∈ (0, ε′) ⊆ (0, ε) and r ∈ (0, δ) with ofReal(K′(rs)ⁿ) < m(ξ, r, s). Since K(rs)ⁿ ≤ K′(rs)ⁿ and ofReal is monotone, ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) ≤ m(ξ, r, s). (⇒) Let K ∈ ℕ and ε ∈ ℚ₊. Apply Φ∞ to K + 1 and ε: there are real s ∈ (0, ε), r ∈ (0, δ) with ofReal((K + 1)(rs)ⁿ) ≤ m(ξ, r, s). As (rs)ⁿ > 0, we get ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) = K(rs)ⁿ < (K + 1)(rs)ⁿ ≤ m(ξ, r, s) = sup_k m(ξ, r_k, s_k), with r_k ↑ r, s_k ↑ s rational as in step 3. Hence some k satisfies m(ξ, r_k, s_k) > ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) ≥ ofReal(K(r_k s_k)ⁿ), using K ≥ 0 and 0 < r_k s_k ≤ rs. Here s_k ∈ (0, ε) and r_k ∈ (0, δ) are rational. Consequently {Φ∞} = ⋂_{K∈ℕ} ⋂_{ε∈ℚ₊} ⋃_{s∈ℚ∩(0,ε)} ⋃_{r∈ℚ∩(0,δ)} {ξ : ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) < m(ξ, r, s)}, which is Borel by step 2.

6. The axis condition. For integers j ≥ 1 let C_j := {(ξ, b) ∈ X × E : b ∈ A, 1/j ≤ |b − αξ| ≤ δ − 1/j, F₁ ξ (b − αξ) = 0}. C_j is closed in X × E: A is closed, (ξ, b) ↦ |b − αξ| is continuous, and (ξ, b) ↦ F₁ ξ (b − αξ) is continuous. Also C_j ⊆ X × A. Because A is compact, the projection X × A → X is a closed map (tube lemma; Mathlib isClosedMap_fst_of_compactSpace). Hence P_j := {ξ : ∃b, (ξ, b) ∈ C_j} is closed in X. (Alternatively, C_j is σ-compact because X × E is proper, so P_j is σ-compact; this is the supplied 1.4(iii).) Moreover {Ax} = ⋃_{j≥1} P_j. If b ∈ A, b ≠ αξ, |b − αξ| < δ and F₁ ξ (b − αξ) = 0, then 0 < |b − αξ| < δ, so 1/j ≤ |b − αξ| ≤ δ − 1/j for all large j. Conversely, 1/j ≤ |b − αξ| ≤ δ − 1/j gives b ≠ αξ and |b − αξ| < δ. Hence {Ax} is an F_σ set, so it is Borel.

7. Conclusion. {ξ : αξ ∈ A} = α⁻¹(A) is closed, since α is continuous and A is closed. Therefore Z = α⁻¹(A) ∖ ({Φ0} ∪ {Φ∞} ∪ {Ax}) is a Boolean combination of Borel sets (steps 4, 5, 6), hence a measurable subset of X. This is the claimed MeasurableSet {ξ : X | α ξ ∈ A ∧ ¬(Φ0 ∨ Φ∞ ∨ Ax)}. ∎
proof_key_steps: ν := Hⁿ⌞A is a finite Borel measure and each generalized cone C(ξ, r, s) is open, so m(ξ, r, s) = ν(C(ξ, r, s)).
For fixed (r, s), ξ ↦ m(ξ, r, s) is lower semicontinuous (Fatou on the open set U ⊆ X × E), hence Borel.
m is monotone in r and s and continuous from below along rational sequences r_k ↑ r, s_k ↑ s (|F₂| > 0 on the cone).
Φ0 and Φ∞ are equivalent to countable rational forms, hence are countable Boolean combinations of Borel sets.
The axis set is the union over j of projections of closed subsets of X × A; these projections are closed because A is compact, so the set is F_σ.
The exceptional set α⁻¹(A) ∖ ({Φ0} ∪ {Φ∞} ∪ {Ax}) is Borel.

subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Step 2.1 (a)–(c) of the supplied proof (Dall'Alba, Lemma 4.15; Mattila Ch. 18), written out. Notation: E := ℝ^{n+ℓ} = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (n+ℓ)), x·y inner product, |·| norm, B(x, ρ) open ball, Hᵐ := μHE[m] (Euclidean Hausdorff measure, an outer measure on all subsets), S(H) := {θ ∈ H : |θ| = 1}, ofReal := ENNReal.ofReal. Two standard facts are used. (L) If f is L-Lipschitz on a set Y (L ≥ 0), then Hⁿ(f(Y)) ≤ Lⁿ Hⁿ(Y) (Mathlib LipschitzOnWith.hausdorffMeasure_image_le for μH[n], and μHE[n] is a positive constant multiple of μH[n]; SimonGMT euclideanHausdorffMeasure_image_le_of_lipschitzOn). (I) Hⁿ(f(Y)) = Hⁿ(Y) for an isometry f (Mathlib Isometry.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_image).

1. Flat balls. Let ℝⁿ := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) and ω_n := Hⁿ(B_{ℝⁿ}(0, 1)). On ℝⁿ, Hⁿ equals Lebesgue measure (Mathlib EuclideanSpace.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_eq_volume), so 0 < ω_n < ∞ (a nonempty bounded open set; n ≥ 1). Also Hⁿ(B_{ℝⁿ}(z, ρ)) = ρⁿω_n for z ∈ ℝⁿ and ρ > 0 (Measure.addHaar_ball). Claim: for every n-dimensional subspace T ⊆ E, every w ∈ T and every ρ > 0, Hⁿ(T ∩ B(w, ρ)) = ω_nρⁿ. Proof: an orthonormal basis of T gives a linear isometry ι : ℝⁿ → E with ι(ℝⁿ) = T. Since ι is isometric onto T, T ∩ B(w, ρ) = ι(B_{ℝⁿ}(ι⁻¹w, ρ)). By (I) the measure is Hⁿ(B_{ℝⁿ}(ι⁻¹w, ρ)) = ω_nρⁿ.

2. Geometry at a point ζ. Fix ζ ∈ S(H). T_ζ := {w ∈ H : w·ζ = 0} is the kernel of the linear functional w ↦ w·ζ on H. This functional is nonzero (ζ·ζ = 1), so dim T_ζ = n. Let π_ζ : E → E be the orthogonal projection onto T_ζ; it is linear with operator norm ≤ 1, hence 1-Lipschitz, and π_ζζ = 0 since ζ ⊥ T_ζ. For ξ ∈ H we have π_ζξ = ξ − (ξ·ζ)ζ. Indeed ξ − (ξ·ζ)ζ ∈ H is orthogonal to ζ, so it lies in T_ζ, and ξ − (ξ − (ξ·ζ)ζ) = (ξ·ζ)ζ is orthogonal to T_ζ. For w ∈ T_ζ with |w| ≤ 1 put f(w) := (1 − |w|²)^{1/2} ∈ [0, 1] and Γ(w) := w + f(w)ζ. Then Γ(w) ∈ H, |Γ(w)|² = |w|² + f(w)² = 1 (w ⊥ ζ), so Γ(w) ∈ S(H), and π_ζΓ(w) = w.

3. Lower bound: c ρⁿ ≤ Hⁿ(S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ)) for 0 < ρ ≤ 2, with c := 2^{−n}ω_n > 0. Let w ∈ T_ζ with |w| < ρ/2 ≤ 1 and put t := |w|² ∈ [0, 1). Since 0 ≤ 1 − t ≤ 1, (1 − t)^{1/2} ≥ 1 − t, so 0 ≤ 1 − f(w) ≤ t and (1 − f(w))² ≤ t² ≤ t. As w ⊥ ζ, |Γ(w) − ζ|² = |w|² + (f(w) − 1)² ≤ 2t = 2|w|² < ρ²/2 < ρ². So Γ(w) ∈ S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ) and w = π_ζ(Γ(w)). Hence T_ζ ∩ B(0, ρ/2) ⊆ π_ζ(S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ)). By (L) with L = 1 and step 1 (T = T_ζ, w = 0): ω_n(ρ/2)ⁿ = Hⁿ(T_ζ ∩ B(0, ρ/2)) ≤ Hⁿ(π_ζ(S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ))) ≤ Hⁿ(S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ)).

4. Upper bound for small radii: Hⁿ(S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ)) ≤ 2ⁿω_nρⁿ for 0 < ρ ≤ 1/2. Let ξ ∈ S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ). Then ξ·ζ = 1 − |ξ − ζ|²/2 > 1 − 1/8 > 0. Put w := π_ζξ = ξ − (ξ·ζ)ζ. Then |w|² = 1 − (ξ·ζ)², so ξ·ζ = f(w) (the positive root) and ξ = Γ(w). Moreover |w| = |π_ζ(ξ − ζ)| ≤ |ξ − ζ| < ρ. Hence S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ) ⊆ Γ(T_ζ ∩ B(0, ρ)). Let D := {w ∈ T_ζ : |w| ≤ 1/2}, which contains T_ζ ∩ B(0, ρ). On D, f ≥ (3/4)^{1/2} = √3/2. For w, w′ ∈ D, |f(w) − f(w′)| = ||w′|² − |w|²|/(f(w) + f(w′)) = (|w| + |w′|)·||w′| − |w||/(f(w) + f(w′)) ≤ 1·|w − w′|/√3 ≤ |w − w′|. Since w − w′ ⊥ ζ, |Γ(w) − Γ(w′)|² = |w − w′|² + (f(w) − f(w′))² ≤ 2|w − w′|². So Γ is 2-Lipschitz on D. By (L) and step 1, Hⁿ(S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ)) ≤ Hⁿ(Γ(T_ζ ∩ B(0, ρ))) ≤ 2ⁿHⁿ(T_ζ ∩ B(0, ρ)) = 2ⁿω_nρⁿ.

5. Hⁿ(S(H)) < ∞. S(H) is closed and bounded in the finite-dimensional space E, hence compact. It is covered by the open balls B(ζ, 1/2), ζ ∈ S(H), so finitely many of them, B(ζ_1, 1/2), …, B(ζ_m, 1/2) with ζ_i ∈ S(H), cover it. By subadditivity and step 4 (with ρ = 1/2), Hⁿ(S(H)) ≤ Σ_i Hⁿ(S(H) ∩ B(ζ_i, 1/2)) ≤ m·2ⁿω_n2^{−n} = mω_n < ∞. Let σ ∈ [0, ∞) be the real number Hⁿ(S(H)).

6. Upper bound for all radii, with C := 2ⁿ max(ω_n, σ). Let ζ ∈ S(H) and ρ > 0. If ρ ≤ 1/2, step 4 gives Hⁿ(S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ)) ≤ 2ⁿω_nρⁿ ≤ Cρⁿ. If ρ > 1/2, then 2ρ > 1, so (2ρ)ⁿ ≥ 1 and Hⁿ(S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ)) ≤ Hⁿ(S(H)) = σ ≤ σ(2ρ)ⁿ = 2ⁿσρⁿ ≤ Cρⁿ.

7. Conclusion. c = 2^{−n}ω_n > 0 and C depend only on n and H, not on ζ or ρ. Steps 3 and 6 give, for every ζ ∈ H with |ζ| = 1 and every ρ > 0: if ρ ≤ 2 then ofReal(cρⁿ) ≤ μHE[n]({θ | θ ∈ H ∧ |θ| = 1} ∩ B(ζ, ρ)); and μHE[n]({θ | θ ∈ H ∧ |θ| = 1} ∩ B(ζ, ρ)) ≤ ofReal(Cρⁿ). ∎
proof_key_steps: Hⁿ(T ∩ B(w, ρ)) = ω_nρⁿ for every n-plane T and w ∈ T (isometry with ℝⁿ, where Hⁿ is Lebesgue measure).

At ζ ∈ S(H), T_ζ := H ∩ ζ^⊥ is n-dimensional. The graph map Γ(w) = w + (1 − |w|²)^{1/2}ζ shows that T_ζ ∩ B(0, ρ/2) ⊆ π_ζ(S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ)). Since π_ζ is 1-Lipschitz, the lower bound 2^{−n}ω_nρⁿ follows for ρ ≤ 2.
For ρ ≤ 1/2, S(H) ∩ B(ζ, ρ) ⊆ Γ(T_ζ ∩ B(0, ρ)) and Γ is 2-Lipschitz on |w| ≤ 1/2, giving the upper bound 2ⁿω_nρⁿ.
Compactness of S(H) and finitely many caps of radius 1/2 give Hⁿ(S(H)) < ∞.
For ρ > 1/2 use Hⁿ(S(H)) ≤ Hⁿ(S(H))(2ρ)ⁿ, and set C := 2ⁿ max(ω_n, Hⁿ(S(H))).

subproblems.title: Sphere lemma: Hⁿ-almost every direction on the unit sphere of an (n+1)-plane is good for the slab cones (Step 2; Dall'Alba Theorem 4.16)
subproblems.statement: Let n ≥ 1, ℓ ∈ ℕ, E := ℝ^{n+ℓ}, H ⊆ E a subspace of dimension n + 1 with orthogonal projection p_H := H.starProjection, A ⊆ E compact with Hⁿ(A) < ∞, δ > 0 and a ∈ E. For θ ∈ E and s > 0 let Z_θ(s) := {x : |p_H(x − a) − (p_H(x − a)·θ)θ| < s|p_H(x − a)|} and m′(θ, r, s) := Hⁿ(A ∩ (Z_θ(s) ∩ B(a, r))). Call θ good if one of the following holds. (Ψ0) For every c > 0 there is ε > 0 with m′(θ, r, s) ≤ c(rs)ⁿ for all 0 < s < ε and 0 < r < δ. (Ψ∞) For every K ∈ ℝ and ε > 0 there are 0 < s < ε and 0 < r < δ with K(rs)ⁿ ≤ m′(θ, r, s). (Ax′) Some b ∈ A has b ≠ a, |b − a| < δ and p_H(b − a) − (p_H(b − a)·θ)θ = 0. Numerical bounds are compared in [0, ∞] via ENNReal.ofReal, and Hⁿ = μHE[n]. Then Hⁿ({θ ∈ H : |θ| = 1 and θ is not good}) = 0.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ), 0 < n → ∀ H : Submodule ℝ (Rn (n + ℓ)), finrank ℝ H = n + 1 → ∀ A : Set (Rn (n + ℓ)), IsCompact A → μHE[n] A < ∞ → ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → ∀ a : Rn (n + ℓ), μHE[n] {θ | θ ∈ H ∧ ‖θ‖ = 1 ∧ ¬ ((∀ c : ℝ, 0 < c → ∃ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε ∧ ∀ s : ℝ, 0 < s → s < ε → ∀ r : ℝ, 0 < r → r < δ → μHE[n] (A ∩ ({x | ‖H.starProjection (x - a) - inner ℝ (H.starProjection (x - a)) θ • θ‖ < s * ‖H.starProjection (x - a)‖} ∩ Metric.ball a r)) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (c * (r * s) ^ n)) ∨ (∀ K : ℝ, ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ s : ℝ, 0 < s ∧ s < ε ∧ ∃ r : ℝ, 0 < r ∧ r < δ ∧ ENNReal.ofReal (K * (r * s) ^ n) ≤ μHE[n] (A ∩ ({x | ‖H.starProjection (x - a) - inner ℝ (H.starProjection (x - a)) θ • θ‖ < s * ‖H.starProjection (x - a)‖} ∩ Metric.ball a r))) ∨ ∃ b ∈ A, b ≠ a ∧ dist b a < δ ∧ H.starProjection (b - a) - inner ℝ (H.starProjection (b - a)) θ • θ = 0)} = 0
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Steps 2.0, 2.2–2.6 of the supplied proof (Dall'Alba, Theorem 4.16 on the sphere; Mattila Ch. 18), written at a general vertex a; the supplied text has a = 0 with A′ = A − a, and all its arguments are applied verbatim with x − a in place of x. Notation: E := ℝ^{n+ℓ}, x·y inner product, |·| norm, B(x, ρ)/B̄(x, ρ) open/closed balls, Hⁿ := μHE[n], p_H := H.starProjection, S(H) := {θ ∈ H : |θ| = 1}, ofReal := ENNReal.ofReal. For θ ∈ E and s > 0, Z_θ(s) := {x : |p_H(x − a) − (p_H(x − a)·θ)θ| < s|p_H(x − a)|} and m′(θ, r, s) := Hⁿ(A ∩ (Z_θ(s) ∩ B(a, r))). θ is good if Ψ0(θ) ∨ Ψ∞(θ) ∨ Ax′(θ), where
 Ψ0(θ): ∀c > 0 ∃ε > 0 ∀s ∈ (0, ε) ∀r ∈ (0, δ): m′(θ, r, s) ≤ ofReal(c(rs)ⁿ);
 Ψ∞(θ): ∀K ∈ ℝ ∀ε > 0 ∃s ∈ (0, ε) ∃r ∈ (0, δ): ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) ≤ m′(θ, r, s);
 Ax′(θ): ∃b ∈ A with b ≠ a, dist(b, a) < δ and p_H(b − a) − (p_H(b − a)·θ)θ = 0.
For y ∈ E and a unit vector θ put d(y, θ) := |y − (y·θ)θ|. This is the distance from y to the line ℝθ, since |y − tθ|² = |y|² − 2t(y·θ) + t² is minimal at t = y·θ. Hence d(ty, θ) = |t|d(y, θ), and d(ξ, θ)² = 1 − (ξ·θ)² for unit ξ.

0. The measure σ_H and the constants. S(H) is closed, hence Borel. σ_H := Hⁿ restricted to S(H), i.e. σ_H(Y) = Hⁿ(Y ∩ S(H)) for every Y ⊆ E, is a Borel measure on E. By the sibling sphere_cap_bounds, i.e. the declaration Submission.bf_sphereCap_measure_bounds (H has dimension n + 1, n ≥ 1), there are c₁ > 0 and C₁ with (a) c₁ρⁿ ≤ σ_H(B(ζ, ρ)) for ζ ∈ S(H) and 0 < ρ ≤ 2, and (b) σ_H(B(ζ, ρ)) ≤ C₁ρⁿ for ζ ∈ S(H) and ρ > 0. S(H) is nonempty (dim H ≥ 1). For any ζ₀ ∈ S(H), S(H) ⊆ B(ζ₀, 3), so σ_H(E) ≤ C₁3ⁿ < ∞; thus σ_H is finite. For θ ∈ S(H) and 0 < ρ ≤ 1: 0 < c₁ρⁿ ≤ σ_H(B(θ, ρ)) ≤ σ_H(B̄(θ, ρ)) ≤ σ_H(B(θ, 2ρ)) ≤ 2ⁿC₁ρⁿ.

1. An outer measure on S(H). For E′ ⊆ S(H) let Λ(E′) := {x ∈ E : p_H(x − a) ≠ 0 and (p_H(x − a)/|p_H(x − a)| ∈ E′ or −p_H(x − a)/|p_H(x − a)| ∈ E′)} and μ(E′) := sup_{0<r<δ} r^{−n}Hⁿ(A ∩ B(a, r) ∩ Λ(E′)) ∈ [0, ∞]. Then μ(∅) = 0 and μ is monotone. μ is countably subadditive: Λ(⋃_i E_i) = ⋃_i Λ(E_i), and for each r, r^{−n}Hⁿ(A ∩ B(a, r) ∩ ⋃_iΛ(E_i)) ≤ Σ_i r^{−n}Hⁿ(A ∩ B(a, r) ∩ Λ(E_i)) ≤ Σ_i μ(E_i); now take the supremum over r. By definition, Hⁿ(A ∩ B(a, r) ∩ Λ(E′)) ≤ rⁿμ(E′) for every r ∈ (0, δ).

2. The axis set. Let C := {θ ∈ S(H) : Ax′(θ)}. For integers j ≥ 1 let K_j := {(θ, b) ∈ S(H) × A : 1/j ≤ |b − a| ≤ δ − 1/j and p_H(b − a) − (p_H(b − a)·θ)θ = 0}. K_j is a closed subset of the compact set S(H) × A (continuous conditions), hence compact, so its first projection π₁(K_j) is compact. Since b ≠ a and |b − a| < δ iff 1/j ≤ |b − a| ≤ δ − 1/j for some j ≥ 1, C = ⋃_j π₁(K_j). So C is σ-compact, hence Borel. Claim: μ(E′) = 0 for every E′ ⊆ S(H) ∖ C. Let r ∈ (0, δ) and suppose x ∈ A ∩ B(a, r) ∩ Λ(E′). Then y := p_H(x − a) ≠ 0, and θ := εy/|y| ∈ E′ for some sign ε ∈ {1, −1}. Then x ≠ a, |x − a| < r < δ, and y = ε|y|θ, so y − (y·θ)θ = 0 (θ is a unit vector). Hence Ax′(θ) holds with b := x, i.e. θ ∈ C, which contradicts θ ∈ E′ ⊆ S(H) ∖ C. So A ∩ B(a, r) ∩ Λ(E′) = ∅ for all r ∈ (0, δ), and μ(E′) = 0. In particular μ(S(H) ∖ C) = 0.

3. Caps versus slab cones. (a) For unit vectors ξ, θ: d(ξ, θ) ≤ |ξ − θ| (θ ∈ ℝθ). If moreover ξ·θ ≥ 0, then |ξ − θ|² = 2 − 2ξ·θ ≤ 2 − 2(ξ·θ)² = 2d(ξ, θ)², since 0 ≤ ξ·θ ≤ 1; hence |ξ − θ| ≤ 2d(ξ, θ). (b) For θ ∈ S(H) and s > 0, Z_θ(s) ⊆ Λ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, 2s)). If x ∈ Z_θ(s), then y := p_H(x − a) ≠ 0 (otherwise the strict inequality would read 0 < 0). Let ξ := εy/|y| with the sign ε ∈ {±1} chosen so that ξ·θ ≥ 0; then ξ ∈ S(H) (y ∈ H) and |ξ − θ| ≤ 2d(ξ, θ) = 2d(y, θ)/|y| < 2s. (c) For θ ∈ S(H) and t > 0, Λ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ⊆ Z_θ(t). If y := p_H(x − a) ≠ 0 and ξ := ±y/|y| ∈ B(θ, t), then d(y, θ) = |y|d(ξ, θ) ≤ |y||ξ − θ| < t|y|.
 Say θ ∈ S(H) satisfies (α) if for every c > 0 there is η > 0 with μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ≤ ofReal(ctⁿ) for all t ∈ (0, η). Say it satisfies (β) if for every K ∈ ℝ and η > 0 there is t ∈ (0, η) with μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) > ofReal(Ktⁿ).
 (α) ⇒ Ψ0(θ): given c > 0 take η for c2^{−n} and put ε := η/2. For s ∈ (0, ε) and r ∈ (0, δ), by (b) and step 1, m′(θ, r, s) ≤ Hⁿ(A ∩ B(a, r) ∩ Λ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, 2s))) ≤ rⁿμ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, 2s)) ≤ rⁿc2^{−n}(2s)ⁿ = c(rs)ⁿ, because 2s < η.
 (β) ⇒ Ψ∞(θ): let K ∈ ℝ and ε > 0. If K ≤ 0, any s ∈ (0, ε), r ∈ (0, δ) work, since ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) = 0. If K > 0, take t ∈ (0, ε) with μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) > Ktⁿ. By definition of the supremum there is r ∈ (0, δ) with r^{−n}Hⁿ(A ∩ B(a, r) ∩ Λ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t))) > Ktⁿ. By (c), m′(θ, r, t) ≥ Hⁿ(A ∩ B(a, r) ∩ Λ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t))) > K(rt)ⁿ. Take s := t.

4. Density dichotomy. Claim: if F ⊆ S(H) is Borel with μ(F) = 0, then the set of θ ∈ F at which neither (α) nor (β) holds is σ_H-null.
 (i) Reduction to closed F. σ_H is a finite Borel measure on the metric space E, hence weakly regular, and closed inner approximation holds (Mathlib MeasurableSet.exists_isClosed_sdiff_lt). So for each k ∈ ℕ there is a closed F̃_k ⊆ F with σ_H(F ∖ F̃_k) < 1/(k+1), and F ∖ ⋃_k F̃_k is σ_H-null. Also μ(F̃_k) ≤ μ(F) = 0. Since (α) and (β) are properties of θ alone, the exceptional set of F is contained in (F ∖ ⋃_kF̃_k) ∪ ⋃_k(exceptional set of F̃_k). So it suffices to treat closed F; from now on F ⊆ S(H) is closed with μ(F) = 0.
 (ii) For integers j ≥ 1 let F_j := {θ ∈ F : μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ≤ jtⁿ for all t ∈ (0, 1/j)}. F_j is closed. Let θ_i ∈ F_j with θ_i → θ; then θ ∈ F. Given t ∈ (0, 1/j) and τ > 0 with t + τ < 1/j, for large i we have |θ_i − θ| < τ, so B(θ, t) ⊆ B(θ_i, t + τ) and μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ≤ j(t + τ)ⁿ. Letting τ ↓ 0 gives μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ≤ jtⁿ. If (β) fails at θ ∈ F, there are K ∈ ℝ and η > 0 with μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ≤ ofReal(Ktⁿ) for all t ∈ (0, η). Then θ ∈ F_j for every integer j ≥ max(K, 1/η, 1), since for t ∈ (0, 1/j) ⊆ (0, η), ofReal(Ktⁿ) ≤ jtⁿ. So it suffices to prove, for each j, that (α) holds at σ_H-a.e. θ ∈ F_j.
 (iii) Covering estimate. Fix j, θ ∈ F_j and t ∈ (0, 1/(10j)). Let R := (S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ∖ F_j. As μ(F_j) ≤ μ(F) = 0, subadditivity gives μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ≤ μ(R) + μ(F_j) = μ(R). If R = ∅ then μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) = 0. Otherwise, for ζ ∈ R put s_ζ := dist(ζ, F_j)/2. Since F_j is closed, ζ ∉ F_j and θ ∈ F_j, we get 0 < s_ζ ≤ |ζ − θ|/2 < t/2. Moreover B(ζ, s_ζ) ⊆ B(θ, 2t) ∖ F_j: for x ∈ B(ζ, s_ζ), |x − θ| < s_ζ + t < 2t and dist(x, F_j) ≥ 2s_ζ − |x − ζ| > 0. By the Vitali covering lemma (Mathlib Vitali.exists_disjoint_subfamily_covering_enlargement applied to the balls B(ζ, s_ζ), ζ ∈ R, with radii in (0, t/2] and τ := 2) there is R′ ⊆ R with two properties. First, the balls B(ζ, s_ζ), ζ ∈ R′, are pairwise disjoint. Second, every ζ ∈ R has some ζ′ ∈ R′ with B(ζ, s_ζ) ∩ B(ζ′, s_ζ′) ≠ ∅ and s_ζ ≤ 2s_ζ′, so |ζ − ζ′| < s_ζ + s_ζ′ ≤ 3s_ζ′ < 5s_ζ′. R′ is countable, being a family of pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets in the separable space E. For ζ ∈ R′, dist(ζ, F_j) = 2s_ζ < 5s_ζ, so there is φ ∈ F_j with |ζ − φ| < 5s_ζ. Then B(ζ, 5s_ζ) ⊆ B(φ, 10s_ζ) with 10s_ζ < 5t < 1/j. Hence μ(S(H) ∩ B(ζ, 5s_ζ)) ≤ μ(S(H) ∩ B(φ, 10s_ζ)) ≤ j(10s_ζ)ⁿ ≤ j10ⁿc₁^{−1}σ_H(B(ζ, s_ζ)), by step 0(a) applied with ζ ∈ S(H) and 0 < s_ζ < 2. R ⊆ ⋃_{ζ∈R′}(S(H) ∩ B(ζ, 5s_ζ)). Apply countable subadditivity of μ, then use that the Borel sets B(ζ, s_ζ), ζ ∈ R′, are disjoint subsets of B(θ, 2t) ∖ F_j: μ(R) ≤ Σ_{ζ∈R′} j10ⁿc₁^{−1}σ_H(B(ζ, s_ζ)) = j10ⁿc₁^{−1}σ_H(⋃_{ζ∈R′}B(ζ, s_ζ)) ≤ j10ⁿc₁^{−1}σ_H(B̄(θ, 2t) ∖ F_j). So μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ≤ j10ⁿc₁^{−1}σ_H(B̄(θ, 2t) ∖ F_j) for θ ∈ F_j and 0 < t < 1/(10j).
 (iv) Density points. By the Lebesgue–Besicovitch density theorem for the finite Borel measure σ_H on E (Mathlib Besicovitch.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div with s := F_j), for σ_H-a.e. θ ∈ F_j the ratio q(ρ) := σ_H(F_j ∩ B̄(θ, ρ))/σ_H(B̄(θ, ρ)) tends to 1 as ρ ↓ 0. Fix such θ ∈ F_j ⊆ S(H). For 0 < ρ ≤ 1, step 0 gives 0 < σ_H(B̄(θ, ρ)) ≤ 2ⁿC₁ρⁿ. As σ_H is finite and F_j is Borel, σ_H(B̄(θ, ρ) ∖ F_j) = σ_H(B̄(θ, ρ)) − σ_H(F_j ∩ B̄(θ, ρ)) = σ_H(B̄(θ, ρ))(1 − q(ρ)) ≤ 2ⁿC₁ρⁿ(1 − q(ρ)). Combine with (iii) and ρ := 2t: for 0 < t < min(1/(10j), 1/2), t^{−n}μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ≤ j10ⁿc₁^{−1}2ⁿC₁2ⁿ(1 − q(2t)), which tends to 0 as t ↓ 0. Hence for every c > 0 there is η > 0 with μ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ≤ ctⁿ for t ∈ (0, η), i.e. (α) holds at θ.
 By (ii)–(iv), {θ ∈ F : neither (α) nor (β)} ⊆ ⋃_{j≥1}{θ ∈ F_j : (α) fails}, a countable union of σ_H-null sets, which proves the claim.

5. Conclusion. F := S(H) ∖ C is Borel (S(H) closed, C Borel), and μ(F) = 0 by step 2. By step 4, N₁ := {θ ∈ F : neither (α) nor (β) holds at θ} is σ_H-null. As N₁ ⊆ S(H), this means Hⁿ(N₁) = σ_H(N₁) = 0. Let θ ∈ S(H) be not good. Then θ ∉ C, since Ax′(θ) fails; so θ ∈ F. Moreover, by step 3, (α) and (β) both fail at θ, because Ψ0(θ) and Ψ∞(θ) fail. So {θ ∈ S(H) : θ not good} ⊆ N₁, and therefore μHE[n]{θ | θ ∈ H ∧ |θ| = 1 ∧ ¬(Ψ0(θ) ∨ Ψ∞(θ) ∨ Ax′(θ))} = 0. ∎
proof_key_steps: σ_H := Hⁿ⌞S(H) is finite, with cap bounds c₁ρⁿ ≤ σ_H(B(ζ, ρ)) ≤ C₁ρⁿ from bf_sphereCap_measure_bounds.
μ(E′) := sup_{0<r<δ} r^{−n}Hⁿ(A ∩ B(a, r) ∩ Λ(E′)), where Λ(E′) is the double cone over E′ ⊆ S(H), is a countably subadditive outer measure on S(H).
The axis set C of directions satisfying Ax′ is σ-compact, and μ(S(H) ∖ C) = 0.
Caps and slab cones are comparable: Z_θ(s) ⊆ Λ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, 2s)) and Λ(S(H) ∩ B(θ, t)) ⊆ Z_θ(t). So vanishing μ-density of caps gives Ψ0, and infinite upper μ-density gives Ψ∞.

Density dichotomy: for a Borel μ-null F ⊆ S(H), at σ_H-a.e. θ ∈ F either μ(caps) = o(tⁿ) or limsup μ(caps)/tⁿ = ∞. The proof uses inner regularity, the closed sets F_j, a Vitali 5r-covering and the Besicovitch density theorem for σ_H.
Apply the dichotomy to F := S(H) ∖ C: every non-good θ lies in a σ_H-null set, hence in an Hⁿ-null set.

subproblems.title: Slab cones versus cones: good slab directions forming an orthonormal basis of W^⊥ give the cone trichotomy (Step 3; Dall'Alba Lemma 5.5)
subproblems.statement: Let n ≥ 1, ℓ ≥ 1, E := ℝ^{n+ℓ}, W ⊆ E an n-dimensional subspace with orthogonal projection P := W.starProjection, u_1, …, u_ℓ orthonormal vectors in W^⊥, and H_j := W ⊔ span{u_j} with orthogonal projection p_j. Let A ⊆ E be any set, δ ∈ ℝ and a ∈ E. Put Z_j(s) := {x : |p_j(x − a) − (p_j(x − a)·u_j)u_j| < s|p_j(x − a)|} and m_j(r, s) := Hⁿ(A ∩ (Z_j(s) ∩ B(a, r))). Suppose that for every j one of the following holds. (Ψ0_j) For every c > 0 there is ε > 0 with m_j(r, s) ≤ c(rs)ⁿ for all 0 < s < ε and 0 < r < δ. (Ψ∞_j) For every K ∈ ℝ and ε > 0 there are 0 < s < ε and 0 < r < δ with K(rs)ⁿ ≤ m_j(r, s). (Ax′_j) Some b ∈ A has b ≠ a, |b − a| < δ and p_j(b − a) − (p_j(b − a)·u_j)u_j = 0. Then the cone trichotomy T(a, P) holds for X(r, s) := {x : |P(x − a)| < s|x − a|} ∩ B(a, r): (Φ0) for every c > 0 there is ε > 0 with Hⁿ(A ∩ X(r, s)) ≤ c(rs)ⁿ for all 0 < s < ε and 0 < r < δ; or (Φ∞) for every K ∈ ℝ and ε > 0 there are 0 < s < ε and 0 < r < δ with K(rs)ⁿ ≤ Hⁿ(A ∩ X(r, s)); or (Ax) some b ∈ A has b ≠ a, |b − a| < δ and P(b − a) = 0. Source: Step 3 (3.1–3.3) of the supplied proof (Dall'Alba, Lemma 5.5, generalized to codimension ℓ), at a general vertex a. The inclusion 3.2(b) is used in the equivalent form X ⊆ ⋃_j Z_j(√ℓ·s), using the bound s* ≤ √ℓ·s of the supplied proof directly. Notation: E := ℝ^{n+ℓ}, x·y inner product, |·| norm, B(x, ρ) open ball, Hⁿ := μHE[n], ofReal := ENNReal.ofReal, P := W.starProjection, H_j := W ⊔ span{u_j} with p_j := H_j.starProjection (j ∈ Fin ℓ). Z_j(s) := {x : |p_j(x − a) − (p_j(x − a)·u_j)u_j| < s|p_j(x − a)|} and m_j(r, s) := Hⁿ(A ∩ (Z_j(s) ∩ B(a, r))). X(s) := {x : |P(x − a)| < s|x − a|} and m(r, s) := Hⁿ(A ∩ (X(s) ∩ B(a, r))). The hypothesis says that for each j, Ψ0_j ∨ Ψ∞_j ∨ Ax′_j holds, where
 Ψ0_j: ∀c > 0 ∃ε > 0 ∀s ∈ (0, ε) ∀r ∈ (0, δ): m_j(r, s) ≤ ofReal(c(rs)ⁿ);
 Ψ∞_j: ∀K ∈ ℝ ∀ε > 0 ∃s ∈ (0, ε) ∃r ∈ (0, δ): ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) ≤ m_j(r, s);
 Ax′_j: ∃b ∈ A with b ≠ a, dist(b, a) < δ and p_j(b − a) − (p_j(b − a)·u_j)u_j = 0.
The goal is Φ0 ∨ Φ∞ ∨ Ax with
 Φ0: ∀c > 0 ∃ε > 0 ∀s ∈ (0, ε) ∀r ∈ (0, δ): m(r, s) ≤ ofReal(c(rs)ⁿ);
 Φ∞: ∀K ∈ ℝ ∀ε > 0 ∃s ∈ (0, ε) ∃r ∈ (0, δ): ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) ≤ m(r, s);
 Ax: ∃b ∈ A with b ≠ a, dist(b, a) < δ and P(b − a) = 0.

1. Orthonormal basis of W^⊥. dim W + dim W^⊥ = dim E = n + ℓ (Mathlib Submodule.finrank_add_finrank_orthogonal), so dim W^⊥ = ℓ. The ℓ orthonormal vectors u_1, …, u_ℓ ∈ W^⊥ are linearly independent, hence an orthonormal basis of W^⊥. For y ∈ E, y − Py ∈ W^⊥ and (y − Py)·u_k = y·u_k because Py ∈ W ⊥ u_k. Hence y − Py = Σ_k(y·u_k)u_k and |y − Py|² = Σ_k(y·u_k)². Since Py ⊥ y − Py, |y|² = |Py|² + Σ_k(y·u_k)².

2. The projection onto H_j. For y ∈ E: p_jy = Py + (y·u_j)u_j. Indeed z := Py + (y·u_j)u_j ∈ H_j. For w ∈ W, (y − z)·w = (y − Py)·w − (y·u_j)(u_j·w) = 0. Also (y − z)·u_j = y·u_j − Py·u_j − (y·u_j)|u_j|² = 0. So y − z is orthogonal to W and to u_j, hence to H_j, and z is the orthogonal projection of y onto H_j. Consequently p_jy·u_j = y·u_j and p_jy − (p_jy·u_j)u_j = Py. Also |p_jy|² = |Py|² + (y·u_j)² ≤ |Py|² + Σ_k(y·u_k)² = |y|² by step 1. Therefore Z_j(s) = {x : |P(x − a)| < s|p_j(x − a)|}, and Ax′_j is equivalent to the existence of b ∈ A with b ≠ a, |b − a| < δ and P(b − a) = 0.

3. Inclusions. Let x ∈ E and y := x − a.
 (a) For s > 0, Z_j(s) ⊆ X(s): if |Py| < s|p_jy|, then |Py| < s|y| because |p_jy| ≤ |y|.
 (b) For s > 0, X(s) ⊆ ⋃_j Z_j(√ℓ·s). Let x ∈ X(s), so 0 ≤ |Py| < s|y| and hence |Py|² < s²|y|². Choose j with (y·u_j)² = max_k(y·u_k)² (ℓ ≥ 1, so Fin ℓ is nonempty); then Σ_k(y·u_k)² ≤ ℓ(y·u_j)². Using ℓ ≥ 1 and step 2: |Py|² < s²(|Py|² + Σ_k(y·u_k)²) ≤ s²(ℓ|Py|² + ℓ(y·u_j)²) = (√ℓ·s)²|p_jy|². Both |Py| and √ℓ·s|p_jy| are ≥ 0, so |Py| < √ℓ·s|p_jy|, i.e. x ∈ Z_j(√ℓ·s).

4. Case analysis. By hypothesis every j satisfies Ψ0_j, Ψ∞_j or Ax′_j.
 Case 1: Ax′_j holds for some j. By step 2 there is b ∈ A with b ≠ a, dist(b, a) < δ and P(b − a) = 0, which is Ax.
 Case 2: Ψ∞_j holds for some j. Let K ∈ ℝ and ε > 0. Ψ∞_j gives s ∈ (0, ε) and r ∈ (0, δ) with ofReal(K(rs)ⁿ) ≤ m_j(r, s). By 3(a), A ∩ (Z_j(s) ∩ B(a, r)) ⊆ A ∩ (X(s) ∩ B(a, r)), so m_j(r, s) ≤ m(r, s) by monotonicity of Hⁿ. This is Φ∞.
 Case 3: otherwise Ψ0_j holds for every j. Let c > 0 and put c′ := c/(ℓ·(√ℓ)ⁿ) > 0. For each j let ε_j > 0 be given by Ψ0_j for the constant c′, and let ε := (min_j ε_j)/√ℓ > 0 (a finite minimum of positive numbers). Let s ∈ (0, ε) and r ∈ (0, δ), and put s′ := √ℓ·s; then 0 < s′ < ε_j for every j. By 3(b), A ∩ (X(s) ∩ B(a, r)) ⊆ ⋃_j A ∩ (Z_j(s′) ∩ B(a, r)). By finite subadditivity of Hⁿ, m(r, s) ≤ Σ_j m_j(r, s′) ≤ Σ_j ofReal(c′(rs′)ⁿ) = ofReal(ℓ·c′·(√ℓ)ⁿ(rs)ⁿ) = ofReal(c(rs)ⁿ). This is Φ0.
 In every case Φ0 ∨ Φ∞ ∨ Ax holds for P = W.starProjection, which is the conclusion. ∎
proof_key_steps: u_1, …, u_ℓ is an orthonormal basis of W^⊥, so |y|² = |Py|² + Σ_k(y·u_k)².
p_jy = Py + (y·u_j)u_j, hence p_jy − (p_jy·u_j)u_j = Py and |p_jy| ≤ |y|; so Ax′_j is Ax.
Z_j(s) ⊆ X(s), and X(s) ⊆ ⋃_j Z_j(√ℓ·s) by choosing j maximizing (y·u_j)².
Case analysis: Ax′_j for some j gives Ax; Ψ∞_j for some j gives Φ∞; otherwise all Ψ0_j hold, and subadditivity with c′ := c/(ℓ·ℓ^{n/2}) gives Φ0.

subproblems.title: Continuity of the frame projection on linearly independent frames (Step 1.5(b))
subproblems.statement: For all N, n ∈ ℕ, consider the map v ↦ frameProjection v = (span{v_1, …, v_n}).starProjection from (ℝ^N)ⁿ = (Fin n → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N)), with the product topology, to the space of continuous linear maps ℝ^N → ℝ^N with the operator-norm topology. This map is continuous on the set of linearly independent frames (ContinuousOn).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (N n : ℕ), ContinuousOn (fun v : Fin n → Rn N ↦ frameProjection v) {v | LinearIndependent ℝ v}
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Step 1.5(b) of the supplied proof (“v ↦ P_v is continuous on 𝒱: if M_v is the N×n matrix with columns v_1, …, v_n, then P_v = M_v(M_vᵀM_v)⁻¹M_vᵀ, and inversion is continuous on invertible matrices”), written out with operators instead of matrices. Notation: E := ℝ^N = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N), F := ℝⁿ = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) with standard basis ε_1, …, ε_n, x·y inner product, |·| norm, T* the adjoint of a continuous linear map between these finite-dimensional inner product spaces, 𝒱 := {v ∈ Eⁿ : v linearly independent}, and frameProjection v = P_{span v} := (span ℝ (range v)).starProjection, the orthogonal projection of E onto span{v_1, …, v_n}.

0. The case n = 0. Then Eⁿ = (Fin 0 → E) has exactly one point, so every function on it is continuous. From now on n ≥ 1 may be assumed, although the argument below does not use it.

1. The frame operator. For v ∈ Eⁿ let M_v : F → E be the linear map M_vc := Σ_i c_iv_i (c = Σ_i c_iε_i). The map v ↦ M_v from Eⁿ to the finite-dimensional normed space 𝓛(F, E) is linear, hence continuous; explicitly ‖M_v − M_w‖ ≤ Σ_i|v_i − w_i|. The adjoint M_v* : E → F is given by (M_v*x)_i = v_i·x. The map T ↦ T* is a linear isometry 𝓛(F, E) → 𝓛(E, F), so v ↦ M_v* is continuous. The Gram operator Γ_v := M_v*M_v ∈ 𝓛(F) has matrix (v_i·v_j)_{i,j}. It depends continuously on v, because composition of continuous linear maps is jointly continuous.

2. Invertibility on 𝒱. Let v ∈ 𝒱. Then M_v is injective (Σ_i c_iv_i = 0 forces c = 0). Hence Γ_v is injective: if Γ_vc = 0 then 0 = c·Γ_vc = M_vc·M_vc = |M_vc|², so M_vc = 0 and c = 0. As F is finite-dimensional, Γ_v is bijective, i.e. a unit of the Banach algebra 𝓛(F), with inverse Γ_v⁻¹.

3. Identification with the orthogonal projection. Let v ∈ 𝒱 and Q_v := M_vΓ_v⁻¹M_v* ∈ 𝓛(E). (a) The range of M_v is span{v_1, …, v_n} = span v. (b) If x ∈ span v, write x = M_vc; then Q_vx = M_vΓ_v⁻¹(M_v*M_vc) = M_vΓ_v⁻¹Γ_vc = M_vc = x. (c) If x ∈ (span v)^⊥, then (M_v*x)_i = v_i·x = 0 for all i, so M_v*x = 0 and Q_vx = 0. The orthogonal projection P_{span v} is likewise the identity on span v and zero on (span v)^⊥. Since E = span v ⊕ (span v)^⊥, Q_v and P_{span v} agree on all of E: Q_v = frameProjection v.

4. Continuity. Let Inv : 𝓛(F) → 𝓛(F) be the ring inverse (Ring.inverse), equal to T⁻¹ on units and 0 elsewhere. On the complete normed ring 𝓛(F), Inv is continuous at every unit (Mathlib NormedRing.inverse_continuousAt). Fix v⁰ ∈ 𝒱. By step 2, Γ_{v⁰} is a unit. By step 1, v ↦ Γ_v is continuous, so v ↦ Inv(Γ_v) is continuous at v⁰. Composition 𝓛(F, E) × 𝓛(F) × 𝓛(E, F) → 𝓛(E), (A, B, C) ↦ A∘B∘C, is continuous. So R(v) := M_v ∘ Inv(Γ_v) ∘ M_v* is continuous at v⁰. For every v ∈ 𝒱, Inv(Γ_v) = Γ_v⁻¹ by step 2, so R(v) = Q_v = frameProjection v by step 3. Hence frameProjection agrees on 𝒱 with a function that is continuous at every point of 𝒱. Therefore, for v⁰ ∈ 𝒱, frameProjection is continuous within 𝒱 at v⁰: ContinuousAt.continuousWithinAt for R, transferred along the equality on 𝒱 (ContinuousWithinAt.congr). This is ContinuousOn (fun v : Fin n → Rn N ↦ frameProjection v) {v | LinearIndependent ℝ v}. ∎

(Remark, not needed for the statement: 𝒱 is open in Eⁿ, see Mathlib isOpen_setOfPred_linearIndependent, or note that v ∈ 𝒱 iff det Γ_v ≠ 0.)
proof_key_steps: The synthesis map M_v : ℝⁿ → ℝ^N, c ↦ Σ c_iv_i, its adjoint and the Gram operator Γ_v = M_v*M_v depend continuously on v.
For linearly independent v, Γ_v is injective, hence invertible.
M_vΓ_v⁻¹M_v* is the identity on span v and zero on (span v)^⊥, so it equals frameProjection v.
Ring inversion is continuous at units, so v ↦ M_v∘Inv(Γ_v)∘M_v* is continuous at each linearly independent frame and agrees with frameProjection there; hence ContinuousOn.

subproblems.title: Averaging over O(N) and transfer to Lebesgue-a.e. frames (Steps 0.2, 4 and 5; Dall'Alba Lemma 5.6)
subproblems.statement: Let n ≥ 1, ℓ ≥ 1, N := n + ℓ, E := ℝ^N = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N), and 𝓛 := E →L[ℝ] E with the Borel σ-algebra of the norm topology. Let μ be a finite measure on E, and let Exc ⊆ E × 𝓛 and Bad ⊆ E × 𝓛 × E be measurable sets. Assume (h1): for every a ∈ E and every (n+1)-dimensional subspace H ⊆ E, Hⁿ({θ ∈ H : |θ| = 1, (a, P_H, θ) ∈ Bad}) = 0, where P_H := H.starProjection and Hⁿ = μHE[n]. Assume (h2): for every a ∈ E, every n-dimensional subspace W with (a, P_W) ∈ Exc, and every orthonormal family u_1, …, u_ℓ of vectors in W^⊥, there is j with (a, P_{W ⊔ span{u_j}}, u_j) ∈ Bad. Then for Lebesgue-a.e. v ∈ Eⁿ, if v is linearly independent then μ({a : (a, frameProjection v) ∈ Exc}) = 0. In other words, ForAlmostAllProjections N n (fun p ↦ μ{a | (a, p) ∈ Exc} = 0).

Source: Steps 0.2, 4.1–4.7, 1.5(b) and 5 of the supplied proof (Dall'Alba, proof of Lemma 5.6; Mattila Ch. 18; the transfer from Haar measure on O(N) to Lebesgue-a.e. frames is the parent's adaptation). The specific exceptional and bad sets of the supplied proof are replaced by the abstract measurable sets Exc and Bad. The supplied Step 4.5 (transport of goodness under h) is then replaced by applying hypothesis (h1) directly to the plane hH⁰.

Notation: N := n + ℓ, E := ℝ^N = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N), x·y inner product, |·| norm, 𝓛 := E →L[ℝ] E with the Borel σ-algebra of its norm topology, g* the adjoint of g ∈ 𝓛, P_V := V.starProjection for a subspace V, Hⁿ := μHE[n]. e_1, …, e_N is the standard basis (e_{n+j} for j ∈ {1, …, ℓ} corresponds to the index Fin.natAdd n j). W₀ := span{e_1, …, e_n}, P₀ := P_{W₀}, H⁰_j := span{e_1, …, e_n, e_{n+j}} = W₀ ⊔ span{e_{n+j}}, H⁰ := H⁰_1, S⁰ := {θ ∈ H⁰ : |θ| = 1}. 𝒱 ⊆ Eⁿ = (Fin n → E) is the set of linearly independent frames, P_v := frameProjection v = P_{span v}, and λ := volume on Eⁿ (the product of the Lebesgue measures of the factors). Exc^p := {a : (a, p) ∈ Exc}.

1. The orthogonal group and its Haar measure (supplied 0.2). Let G := {g ∈ 𝓛 : g*g = 1}. Each g ∈ G is a linear isometry, since |gx|² = x·g*gx = |x|². So g is injective, hence bijective (finite dimension), with g⁻¹ = g*; thus also gg* = 1. G is a subgroup of the invertible elements of 𝓛, and g* = g⁻¹ ∈ G. G is closed in 𝓛, being the preimage of {1} under the continuous map g ↦ g*g. It is bounded (‖g‖ ≤ 1), hence compact because 𝓛 is finite-dimensional. (Lean hint: G can be realized as unitary 𝓛 for the star ring 𝓛, star = adjoint. Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Star/Unitary.lean, which must then be imported, gives IsTopologicalGroup (unitary R) and isClosed_unitary under [ContinuousStar R]. For 𝓛 this instance is not inferred automatically; supply it from the continuity of ContinuousLinearMap.adjoint. Compactness, i.e. CompactSpace G, is not a library instance and is proved from closed + bounded as above.) Multiplication and inversion (= adjoint) are continuous. So G is a compact, second-countable, metrizable topological group; give it its Borel σ-algebra (the trace of that of 𝓛).
 There is a left-invariant Borel probability measure θ_N on G: the Haar measure normalized by θ_N(G) = 1 (Mathlib haarMeasure with K₀ = G and haarMeasure_self). θ_N is also right invariant. For k ∈ G let ρ_k be the image of θ_N under g ↦ gk⁻¹, so ρ_k(B) = θ_N(Bk). ρ_k is a finite left-invariant Borel measure, because left and right translations commute. By uniqueness of Haar measure on compact groups (Mathlib isMulInvariant_eq_smul_of_compactSpace), ρ_k = c·θ_N for a constant c ≥ 0. Comparing total masses, c = θ_N(Gk) = θ_N(G) = 1. (Equivalently, ρ_k and θ_N are left-invariant Haar probability measures, so they coincide by Mathlib Measure.isHaarMeasure_eq_of_isProbabilityMeasure.) Likewise G′ := {g ∈ G : ge_k = e_k for k = n + 2, …, N} is a closed subgroup of G, hence a compact topological group, and it carries a left- and right-invariant Borel probability measure θ′ (same argument).
 Basic facts. (F1) For g ∈ G and a subspace V, gV is a subspace with dim gV = dim V and P_{gV} = gP_Vg*: gP_Vg* is self-adjoint and idempotent, and its range is g(range P_V) = gV. (F2) If g ∈ G′ then gH⁰ = H⁰ and gS⁰ = S⁰. Indeed H⁰ = span{e_{n+2}, …, e_N}^⊥. For x ∈ H⁰ and k ≥ n + 2, gx·e_k = gx·ge_k = x·e_k = 0, so g maps H⁰ into H⁰, and onto it by dimension count; and g is isometric. (F3) The maps g ↦ gPg* (P ∈ 𝓛 fixed) and g ↦ gx (x ∈ E fixed) are continuous on G, (g, x) ↦ gx is continuous on G × E, and (g, v) ↦ g·v := (gv_1, …, gv_n) is continuous on G × Eⁿ.

2. Bad planes give bad directions (supplied 4.1). Fix a ∈ E and let g ∈ G. W := gW₀ has dimension n and P_W = gP₀g* (F1). The vectors u_j := ge_{n+j}, j ∈ {1, …, ℓ}, are orthonormal (g is isometric) and lie in W^⊥: for w₀ ∈ W₀, ge_{n+j}·gw₀ = e_{n+j}·w₀ = 0. Also W ⊔ span{u_j} = g(W₀ ⊔ span{e_{n+j}}) = gH⁰_j, so P_{W⊔span{u_j}} = gP_{H⁰_j}g* (F1). Let B_j(a) := {g ∈ G : (a, gP_{H⁰_j}g*, ge_{n+j}) ∈ Bad}. By (h2), applied to a, W and u: if (a, gP₀g*) ∈ Exc, then g ∈ B_j(a) for some j. Each B_j(a) is Borel in G, as the preimage of the measurable set Bad ⊆ E × 𝓛 × E under the continuous map g ↦ (a, gP_{H⁰_j}g*, ge_{n+j}) (F3). On these second-countable spaces the product σ-algebra is the Borel σ-algebra.

3. Reduction to j = 1 (supplied 4.3). Let σ_j ∈ G be the permutation of the basis exchanging e_{n+1} and e_{n+j} and fixing the other e_k (σ_1 := 1). Then σ_jH⁰_1 = H⁰_j and σ_je_{n+1} = e_{n+j}. Hence for g ∈ G, (gσ_j)P_{H⁰_1}(gσ_j)* = gP_{σ_jH⁰_1}g* = gP_{H⁰_j}g* (F1) and (gσ_j)e_{n+1} = ge_{n+j}. So g ∈ B_j(a) ⟺ gσ_j ∈ B_1(a), i.e. B_j(a) = B_1(a)σ_j⁻¹. By right invariance, θ_N(B_j(a)) = θ_N(B_1(a)).

4. The law of g′e_{n+1} (supplied 4.4). The sibling sphere_cap_bounds, i.e. the declaration Submission.bf_sphereCap_measure_bounds, applies to H⁰ (dimension n + 1, n ≥ 1) and gives constants c > 0, C. With ζ := e_{n+1} ∈ S⁰: Hⁿ(S⁰) ≥ Hⁿ(S⁰ ∩ B(e_{n+1}, 2)) ≥ c2ⁿ > 0. Since S⁰ ⊆ B(e_{n+1}, 3), Hⁿ(S⁰) = Hⁿ(S⁰ ∩ B(e_{n+1}, 3)) ≤ C3ⁿ < ∞. So σ̄(B) := Hⁿ(B ∩ S⁰)/Hⁿ(S⁰), for Borel B ⊆ E, is a Borel probability measure on E with σ̄(E ∖ S⁰) = 0. Let ν₀ be the image of θ′ under the continuous map g′ ↦ g′e_{n+1}; by (F2) it is a Borel probability measure on E with ν₀(E ∖ S⁰) = 0. Claim: ν₀ = σ̄.
 (a) Invariance. Let k ∈ G′ and B Borel. ν₀(k⁻¹B) = θ′({g′ : kg′e_{n+1} ∈ B}) = θ′(k⁻¹{g′ : g′e_{n+1} ∈ B}) = ν₀(B) by left invariance of θ′. Also σ̄(k⁻¹B) = Hⁿ(k⁻¹B ∩ S⁰)/Hⁿ(S⁰) = Hⁿ(k⁻¹(B ∩ S⁰))/Hⁿ(S⁰) = σ̄(B), because k⁻¹S⁰ = S⁰ (F2) and Hⁿ is invariant under the isometry k⁻¹ (Mathlib Isometry.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_image).
 (b) Transitivity. Let x, y ∈ S⁰. If x = y take k := 1. Otherwise put d := x − y ≠ 0 and k z := z − 2((z·d)/|d|²)d, the reflection in d^⊥; k ∈ G (k* = k, k² = 1). Since |x| = |y| = 1, y·d = y·x − 1 = −|d|²/2, so ky = y + d = x. For i ≥ n + 2, e_i·d = 0 (d ∈ H⁰), so ke_i = e_i and k ∈ G′.
 (c) Uniqueness. Let ν be any Borel probability measure on E with ν(E ∖ S⁰) = 0 and ν(k⁻¹B) = ν(B) for all k ∈ G′ and Borel B. Let φ : E → ℝ be bounded and continuous, and Ψ(x) := ∫_{G′}φ(g′x) dθ′(g′). By invariance, ∫_Eφ(g′x) dν(x) = ∫φ dν for each g′ ∈ G′. Integrate over g′ (θ′ is a probability) and apply Fubini to the bounded continuous function (g′, x) ↦ φ(g′x) and the finite measure θ′ ⊗ ν: ∫φ dν = ∫_{G′}∫_Eφ(g′x) dν(x) dθ′(g′) = ∫_EΨ(x) dν(x). For x, y ∈ S⁰ take k from (b); by right invariance of θ′, Ψ(x) = Ψ(ky) = ∫φ(g′ky) dθ′(g′) = ∫φ(g′y) dθ′(g′) = Ψ(y). So Ψ is constant on S⁰, equal to Ψ(e_{n+1}). As ν(E ∖ S⁰) = 0 and ν(E) = 1, ∫φ dν = Ψ(e_{n+1}), a value independent of ν. Applying this to ν₀ and σ̄ gives ∫φ dν₀ = ∫φ dσ̄ for every bounded continuous φ. Hence ν₀ = σ̄, since finite Borel measures on a metric space are determined by the integrals of bounded continuous functions (Mathlib MeasureTheory.ext_of_forall_integral_eq_of_IsFiniteMeasure, in Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/HasOuterApproxClosed.lean, which must be imported).
 Consequence: for every Borel Y ⊆ E with Hⁿ(Y ∩ S⁰) = 0, θ′({g′ ∈ G′ : g′e_{n+1} ∈ Y}) = ν₀(Y) = σ̄(Y) = 0.

5. Fibres over cosets (supplied 4.5). Fix a ∈ E and h ∈ G, and let H := hH⁰. H has dimension n + 1 and P_H = hP_{H⁰}h* (F1). For g′ ∈ G′, hg′H⁰ = hH⁰ = H (F2), so (hg′)P_{H⁰}(hg′)* = P_H. Thus hg′ ∈ B_1(a) ⟺ (a, P_H, hg′e_{n+1}) ∈ Bad ⟺ g′e_{n+1} ∈ Y_h := h⁻¹(Bad_{a,H}), where Bad_{a,H} := {θ ∈ E : (a, P_H, θ) ∈ Bad} is Borel (a section of a measurable set). Y_h = h*(Bad_{a,H}) is Borel, h* being a homeomorphism. Since h⁻¹ maps S(H) := {θ ∈ H : |θ| = 1} = hS⁰ onto S⁰, Y_h ∩ S⁰ = h⁻¹(Bad_{a,H} ∩ S(H)). By isometry invariance of Hⁿ and hypothesis (h1) for a and H: Hⁿ(Y_h ∩ S⁰) = Hⁿ(Bad_{a,H} ∩ S(H)) = Hⁿ({θ | θ ∈ H ∧ |θ| = 1 ∧ (a, P_H, θ) ∈ Bad}) = 0. By step 4, θ′({g′ ∈ G′ : hg′ ∈ B_1(a)}) = θ′({g′ : g′e_{n+1} ∈ Y_h}) = 0.

6. Fubini (supplied 4.6). Let χ := 1_{B_1(a)}. The map (h, g′) ↦ χ(hg′) is Borel on G × G′, because B_1(a) is Borel and multiplication is continuous. For each g′ ∈ G′ ⊆ G, right invariance gives ∫_Gχ(hg′) dθ_N(h) = θ_N(B_1(a)g′⁻¹) = θ_N(B_1(a)). Integrate over g′ (θ′(G′) = 1) and apply Tonelli to θ_N ⊗ θ′: θ_N(B_1(a)) = ∫_{G′}∫_Gχ(hg′) dθ_N(h) dθ′(g′) = ∫_G∫_{G′}χ(hg′) dθ′(g′) dθ_N(h) = 0 by step 5. By steps 2 and 3, θ_N({g ∈ G : (a, gP₀g*) ∈ Exc}) ≤ Σ_jθ_N(B_j(a)) = ℓ·θ_N(B_1(a)) = 0. This holds for every a ∈ E.

7. Tonelli over E × G (supplied 4.7). 𝒩′ := {(a, g) ∈ E × G : (a, gP₀g*) ∈ Exc} is measurable, being the preimage of Exc under the continuous map (a, g) ↦ (a, gP₀g*). Apply Tonelli to the finite measures μ and θ_N: ∫_Gμ({a : (a, g) ∈ 𝒩′}) dθ_N(g) = ∫_Eθ_N({g : (a, g) ∈ 𝒩′}) dμ(a) = 0 by step 6. Hence μ(Exc^{gP₀g*}) = 0 for θ_N-a.e. g. The map p ↦ μ(Exc^p) is measurable on 𝓛 by the measurability part of Tonelli for the finite measure μ and the measurable set Exc (Mathlib measurable_measure_prodMk_right). So 𝒢 := {p ∈ 𝓛 : μ(Exc^p) > 0} is Borel, 𝒢̃ := {g ∈ G : gP₀g* ∈ 𝒢} is Borel, and θ_N(𝒢̃) = 0.

8. Measurability of the bad frames (supplied 1.5(b)). 𝒱 is open in Eⁿ (Mathlib isOpen_setOfPred_linearIndependent; equivalently, v ∈ 𝒱 iff the Gram determinant det(v_i·v_j) is nonzero). By the sibling frame_projection_continuous, i.e. the declaration Submission.bf_frameProjection_continuousOn, v ↦ P_v = frameProjection v is continuous on 𝒱. Hence 𝒮 := {v ∈ 𝒱 : P_v ∈ 𝒢} = 𝒱 ∩ (P|_𝒱)⁻¹(𝒢) is Borel in Eⁿ: the preimage of the Borel set 𝒢 under a map continuous on the open set 𝒱, intersected with 𝒱, is Borel (Mathlib ContinuousOn.measurable_piecewise, or directly: (P|_𝒱)⁻¹(U) is relatively open in 𝒱, hence open in Eⁿ, for every open U ⊆ 𝓛, so the class of Borel B with 𝒱 ∩ (P|_𝒱)⁻¹(B) Borel is a σ-algebra containing the open sets).

9. Transfer to frames (supplied 5.1–5.3). (a) For g ∈ G, v ↦ g·v preserves λ. On each factor, g is a linear isometry equivalence of E and so preserves its volume (Mathlib LinearIsometryEquiv.measurePreserving); hence the product map preserves λ (measurePreserving_pi). If v ∈ 𝒱 then g·v ∈ 𝒱, span(g·v) = g(span v), and P_{g·v} = gP_vg* (F1). If v ∉ 𝒱 then g·v ∉ 𝒱, as g is injective. (b) Let v ∈ 𝒱. Choose an orthonormal basis f_1, …, f_n of span v and extend it by an orthonormal basis f_{n+1}, …, f_N of (span v)^⊥. The linear map h with he_k = f_k lies in G and hW₀ = span v. So P_v = hP₀h*, and P_{g·v} = (gh)P₀(gh)* for g ∈ G. Hence {g ∈ G : g·v ∈ 𝒮} = {g : gh ∈ 𝒢̃} = 𝒢̃h⁻¹, and θ_N({g : g·v ∈ 𝒮}) = θ_N(𝒢̃) = 0 by right invariance and step 7. For v ∉ 𝒱 the set {g : g·v ∈ 𝒮} is empty, since 𝒮 ⊆ 𝒱. (c) The set {(g, v) ∈ G × Eⁿ : g·v ∈ 𝒮} is Borel (F3, step 8). By (a), λ({v : g·v ∈ 𝒮}) = λ(𝒮) for every g ∈ G. Using θ_N(G) = 1, Tonelli (θ_N finite, λ σ-finite) and (b): λ(𝒮) = ∫_Gλ({v : g·v ∈ 𝒮}) dθ_N(g) = ∫_{Eⁿ}θ_N({g : g·v ∈ 𝒮}) dλ(v) = 0.

10. Conclusion. λ(𝒮) = 0, so for λ-a.e. v ∈ Eⁿ we have v ∉ 𝒮. That is, if v is linearly independent then frameProjection v ∉ 𝒢, i.e. μ({a | (a, frameProjection v) ∈ Exc}) = 0. This is ForAlmostAllProjections (n + ℓ) n (fun p ↦ μ {a | (a, p) ∈ Exc} = 0). ∎
proof_key_steps: O(N) = {g ∈ 𝓛 : g*g = 1} is a compact metrizable group with a bi-invariant Haar probability θ_N (right invariance follows from uniqueness of Haar measure). Likewise the stabilizer O′ of e_{n+2}, …, e_N carries such a measure θ′.
For g ∈ O(N), W = gW₀ and u_j = ge_{n+j} fall under (h2), so {g : (a, gP₀g*) ∈ Exc} ⊆ ⋃_j B_j(a) with Borel sets B_j(a). A basis permutation and right invariance give θ_N(B_j(a)) = θ_N(B_1(a)).

The law of g′e_{n+1} under θ′ is normalized Hⁿ on S⁰. Here 0 < Hⁿ(S⁰) < ∞ by bf_sphereCap_measure_bounds, and uniqueness follows from invariance, transitivity via reflections, Fubini and right invariance.
Fibres over cosets hO′ are θ′-null by (h1) for H = hH⁰ and isometry invariance of Hⁿ. Fubini with right invariance then gives θ_N(B_1(a)) = 0, hence θ_N{g : (a, gP₀g*) ∈ Exc} = 0 for every a.
Tonelli over μ ⊗ θ_N gives θ_N{g : μ(Exc^{gP₀g*}) > 0} = 0, where 𝒢 = {p : μ(Exc^p) > 0} is Borel.
Transfer: the bad-frame set 𝒮 is Borel by bf_frameProjection_continuousOn. Lebesgue measure on frames is O(N)-invariant and θ_N{g : g·v ∈ 𝒮} = 0 for every v, so Tonelli gives λ(𝒮) = 0.
